"For as long as life lasts, abstaining from false speech is a training rule for a lay follower. What, then, is false speech? Thus it was said by the Blessed One: [text follows].

Whether he has gone to an assembly, or is in the midst of a crowd, or in the midst of a royal court, or in the midst of a council, or in the midst of his kinsmen, being questioned as a witness, [he says]: "O man, what you know, speak that;
what you do not know, do not say."
Do not say this: that he, while not knowing at all, says "I know";
while not seeing at all, says "I see";
while actually knowing, says "I do not know"; while actually seeing, says "I do not see"—whether for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for some trifling material gain.

“He is one who does not abstain from false speech” means that because of this false speech he is not devoted to it, has not desisted from it, is not restrained from it, and does not refrain from it; being established therein, he is possessed of it.
Therefore it is said: “He is indeed a speaker of falsehood.
Or, “from an assembly,” etc.
...the royal assembly and the public assembly;
he has gone there, has arrived, is present, and is face-to-face with them; therefore, it is said that "he has gone to the assembly."
"Or having entered an assembly" refers to the four assemblies, namely: the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas... [and so forth].
He has gone there, arrived, entered, and become present; therefore, it is said that he "has gone to the assembly."
Or, as for "having entered into the midst of the royal court," it means that the assembly of the king’s ministers is seated together.
Because he has come together, assembled, and appeared in person, it is said: "having entered into the midst of the royal court."
Or, being situated in the midst of an appropriate family, an appropriate assembly is seated together and gathered there. In that [assembly], he...
Because that which is beneficial has become manifest, it is said: "having entered among families of practitioners."
"Or, having gone into the midst of his kinsmen," he says: "his kinsmen are seated together and assembled there, and he has gone to that place."
Because he has come face-to-face with them, it is said: "having entered into the midst of his kinsmen."
"Being questioned as a witness" means that the witness has been requested, approached, or summoned;
[the phrase] "O man! means "come here," "approach," or "exert yourself."

“...do not designate, do not establish, do not reveal that which has not been seen, not heard, not thought, and not cognized; with effort, do not speak of it, do not teach it, do not designate it, do not establish it, and do not reveal it.
He, being without knowledge, [falsely] conceives...”

He says, "I have not heard it. Having set aside the perception, having set aside the acceptance, the preference, the thought, the examination, and the view regarding that which was experienced by ear-consciousness and cognized by ear-consciousness, he says, "I have not heard it.
Thus, even while not knowing, he says, "I perceive it."

18. (Loving-kindness as mental concentration: That which is conducive to liberation, appropriate, favorable, and [possessing] the equipment of the limbs—this mind, for the time being, should be called loving-kindness as mental concentration (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*).
The mind and mental consciousness of one who has thus attained meditative absorption are called "the mind accompanied by loving-kindness. Whatever volition, intention,
thorough intention, that which is intended, what belongs to volition, the mental formations of the mind, and mental action— this is called "action co-arising with loving-kindness."
That which is the mental resolve, the inclination, and the state of being inclined of the mind— this is called the resolve co-arising with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Furthermore, whatever feeling, perception, desire, affection, attention, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom belongs to one who has thus attained meditative absorption— these factors as well are co-arising with loving-kindness.
All these factors should be called the concentration of the mind on loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*).
Indeed, this concentration of the mind on loving-kindness is twofold:
limited and immeasurable.
What is the application for the limited concentration of mind on loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*)?
And how, when so applied, does one enter into the limited concentration of mind on loving-kindness? It is said:
Just as, in this world, there are certain beings who are dear, beloved, pleasing, and agreeable to someone...
For example, toward a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or any other friend, kinsman, or blood relative—
he establishes, settles, tames, calms, thoroughly pacifies, makes one-pointed, and concentrates his limited mind, which is conjoined with limited loving-kindness, upon these limited sentient beings.

As he establishes, settles, stabilizes, tames, pacifies, thoroughly calms, unifies, and concentrates his limited mind—concomitant with loving-kindness—upon those limited sentient beings, that mind becomes distracted, wanders away, runs off, does not become one-pointed, and single-minded mindfulness does not remain established.
That his mind becomes distracted, wanders away, and runs off [is due to the thought]: "O, how happy these limited sentient beings are!"
He does not become one-pointed; his mindfulness does not abide in a single focus.

Thinking, "How limited indeed are these beings who are happy," he has not attained a state of one-pointedness, nor has he entered the concentration of a limited friendly mind (*maitra-cetasaḥ-samādhi*);
thus it should be said.
As that mind becomes distracted, wanders away, and runs about, he draws it back to that very [object]; he attends to that very sign:
"Alas, how happy are beings! For one who attends in this way, whatever energy, exertion, departure, valor, strength, undertaking, enthusiasm, perseverance, and lack of despondency there is—

Furthermore, regarding this application of the limited concentration of the mind on loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetasaḥ-samādhi*): having applied himself in this way, he enters into that limited concentration of the mind on loving-kindness.
He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that arisen path; for him, this is the path.
As he cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices it, that mind becomes steady, well-settled, present, one-pointed, and concentrated.

And because that mind has become steady, well-settled, present, non-dual, and undiminished, he enters upon this limited concentration of the mind of loving-kindness, thinking: "O, how happy these beings are!
This much is the limited concentration of the mind of loving-kindness.
Thus it should be stated:
for one who has thus attained meditative absorption, that mind which is mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is called "limited" (*parītta*) and is co-existent with loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
as for the volition (*cetanā*) within that mind, and so forth in detail, up to...
These factors also arise together with limited loving-kindness;
all these factors should be called "limited concentration of the mind on loving-kindness. What, then, is the application for the immeasurable concentration of the mind on loving-kindness?
And how, moreover, does one who is thus engaged attain the immeasurable meditative concentration of loving-kindness?

Having tamed, directed, warmed, thoroughly warmed, straightened, made supple and workable, made upright, clear, and compliant that very mind which was previously practiced in limited loving-kindness, [one attains it].

Thereafter, [the thought] "O, how happy are sentient beings! gradually pervades immeasurably the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions. As he thus pervades the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions with the thought, "O, how happy are sentient beings!", that mind becomes distracted, scattered, and runs about; it does not become one-pointed, nor does it become focused on a single object.
Mindfulness becomes established:

"O, how immeasurable is the happiness of sentient beings! From the moment his mind is distracted by that [thought], and so on in detail until [the distraction ceases], to that extent he should be said to have entered the concentration of the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*).
As that mind becomes distracted, wanders away, and runs about, he draws it back to that very [object],
and attends to that very thing with his attention.

"O, how happy are sentient beings!"—for one who attends to [them] in this way, whatever vigor there is, and so forth in detail, up to: "this is the application in the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetaḥsamādhi*).
And when thus applied, he has entered the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness.
Thus it should be said:
for one who has thus attained meditative absorption, that which is the mind and mental consciousness is called the immeasurable mind co-arising with loving-kindness;
[this includes] whatever volition there is, and so forth, in detail, up to...
These factors as well coexist with immeasurable loving-kindness;
therefore, all these factors should be called "immeasurable loving-kindness, the concentration of mind."
19. (Compassion as Mental Concentration) What is compassion? It is said: [the answer follows].

"Alas, beings are suffering!"— this [thought] which is born of seclusion, arisen internally, produced through discernment, wholesome, associated with the form realm, characterized by distress and distressing, suffering and causing suffering, compassion and causing compassion, and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with that compassion, as well as the bodily action and vocal action arising therefrom, and the formations dissociated from mind that arise from those— [these are the formations associated with the form realm].
This is called compassion.
And [it is] immeasurable.

What is the application (*prayoga*) of the limited concentration of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-cetasaḥ-samādhi*)? And how does one, having applied oneself, enter into the limited concentration of the mind of compassion? He said: Just as here, a certain person—namely, a mother, or a father, or a brother, or a sister, or any other friend, relative, or kinsman—with these [objects], [cultivates] a limited [state] accompanied by compassion...
He settles the mind, he settles it thoroughly...

...he calms it, makes it one-pointed, and concentrates it, [thinking]: "Alas, beings are limited and suffering! As he thus establishes, tames, and pacifies his mind—which is limited and accompanied by compassion—by means of these limited [mental states]...
From that, that mind becomes distracted; the details are as stated in the [section on] loving-kindness (maitrī).
What is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? It is said: for one who attends to the thought, "O, may sentient beings rejoice," that which consists of renunciation and seclusion...
Wholesome states associated with the form realm: the gladdening of the mind, rejoicing, intense rejoicing;
joy, gladness, mental uplift, cheerfulness, satisfaction, and exertion.
The state of being uplifted by joy is *prīti*; the state of being pervaded by *prīti* is called *muditā*.

Furthermore, *muditā* consists of the feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) associated with *muditā*, as well as whatever arises from them.
The formations dissociated from [the aforementioned] are called sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

Indeed, sympathetic joy is a concentration of mind (*cetaḥsamādhi*) that is twofold: limited (*parītta*) and immeasurable (*apramāṇa*). What is the application for the limited concentration of mind of sympathetic joy?

...he enters into concentration. He said: "Just as, for instance, there are certain beings here who are desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing to someone—such as a mother, or a father, or a brother, or a sister, or any other [relative]..."

With these limited sentient beings, he establishes, settles, fixes, tames, calms, pacifies, thoroughly pacifies, unifies, and concentrates his limited mind that is concomitant with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
As he establishes, settles, stabilizes, tames, pacifies, thoroughly calms, unifies, and concentrates his mind— accompanied by limited sympathetic joy toward those limited beings—
that mind becomes distracted.
For one who attends to [beings] as "most wretched beings," there arises— born of renunciation and seclusion, arisen through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
produced by discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*)— a wholesome equanimity of mind, clarity of mind, and non-distraction of the mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

And that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness associated with equanimity, as well as the bodily action and vocal action arising therefrom, and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom—
this is called equanimity. What is the preparatory application?
Furthermore, he enters into equanimity and concentration; it is said:
"Just as, indeed, there are certain beings here who are desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the mind—such as a mother, or a father, or a brother, or a sister, or any other such [relative]..."

It occurs to him: "This is my mother, or my father, or my brother, or my sister, or some other relative, friend, kinsman, or blood relation; or, at least, he is a sentient being. Thus he becomes resolved upon [the person], just as, for example, ...

There he might see *sāla* trees, or *tāla* trees, or *naktamāla* trees, or *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, and *nyagrodha* trees; it does not occur to him, "These here are *sāla* trees, or *tāla* trees, or *naktamāla* trees, or *aśvattha*, *udumbara*..."
He becomes liberated.

In the same way, for a certain person here, regarding those beings who are dear and beloved—extensively, including kinsmen and blood relations—it does not occur to him: "This is my mother," or "This is my father," or "This is my brother," and so forth.

Or, whether one is a relative up to the third degree, or indeed any other being, one becomes resolved that "this is a being"; this is the application. And for one thus engaged, the meditative concentration of equanimity of the mind is accomplished; such is the meditative concentration of equanimity of the mind.
And it is both limited and immeasurable.

What is the application for the limited concentration of mind associated with equanimity? And how does one apply oneself so as to enter into the limited concentration of mind associated with equanimity? He said:
"Just as, indeed, in this case, for a certain person..."
In detail, up to his kinsmen and blood relations— he, with these limited beings, establishes, settles, fixes, tames, and pacifies a limited mind accompanied by equanimity.
